idiom_name: std::unordered_map + std::list splice LRU under a std::mutex (no stdlib cache)
implementation_notes: The standard library supplies the container pair but no cache: the classic realization stores entries in a std::list (MRU at the front) and keeps a std::unordered_map from key to list iterator, so a hit is one splice() to the front and a capacity overflow is one pop_back() - both O(1). References and pointers into std::unordered_map survive rehashing (only iterators are invalidated), which is what makes the map/list split safe; C++17 adds try_emplace/insert_or_assign for miss population and node extract() for moving entries without reallocation. Concurrency stays hand-written: a std::mutex (or sharded mutexes) guards both containers in one critical section, and std::shared_ptr values are the answer when eviction can race with readers that hold a reference. Neither Boost nor Abseil ships a cache, so unless a third-party cache is adopted the structure is written in-project.
pitfalls: Erasing from the map and splicing the list in the wrong order - or outside one critical section - leaves dangling iterators; mutate both containers under the same lock.
std::shared_mutex looks attractive for a read-mostly cache, but every LRU hit mutates the recency list, so hits need exclusive access anyway; sharding beats reader/writer locks here.
unordered_map rehash invalidates iterators (not references), so storing iterators is safe while storing raw pointers into list nodes is safe only until that node is erased.
Caching polymorphic values by value slices them; store std::shared_ptr<Base> (or std::variant) instead.
